prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Business software subscription pricing (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Plan" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Price" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Minimum seats" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Contract" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Support" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Plan" · longest unbreakable word 75px · one-line width 75px
  col 2: header "Price › List price" · longest unbreakable word 37px · one-line width 67px
  col 3: header "Price › Billing terms" · longest unbreakable word 86px · one-line width 490px
  col 4: header "Minimum seats" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 109px
  col 5: header "Contract" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 123px
  col 6: header "Support" · longest unbreakable word 79px · one-line width 195px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 707px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 706px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"Billing terms is the longest content but gets a narrow column, wrapping into 5–7 lines and making rows very tall; Support is over-wide with dead space, so proportions and scanning rhythm fail."},"B":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Billing terms is generously wide and rows stay compact, but the 'List price' header wraps awkwardly and Support is squeezed narrower than Contract despite longer text."},"C":{"grade":"good","why":"Billing terms gets the dominant share and headers mostly fit, but Support is narrower than Contract and wraps into three-line stacks, slightly weakening comparison."},"D":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Best balance: Billing terms remains clearly widest, Support is wider than Contract and wraps less, List price header fits, and the shorter columns stay proportionate."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Very close to the best: Billing terms is well served, but Support remains slightly narrower than Contract and some support cells still stack into three lines."},"F":{"grade":"poor","why":"Billing terms is starved while List price, Contract and Support are over-wide, producing excessive wrapping and tall, uneven rows."}},"best":["D"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"C, D and E are close and exact rendered widths are hard to measure; the choice depends on whether Billing terms width or reduced Support wrapping matters more."}
